CURRENT PHASE: ios_architecture_review
PHASE PURPOSE: Review the app as an iOS product before final tech specs: SwiftUI architecture, Apple framework choices, local persistence, privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit/subscription architecture, permissive dependency policy, and testability.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS spaced-repetition flashcard app called "Recall". Native Apple stack ONLY: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, Swift Charts for stats. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network of any kind — the app must work in airplane mode forever, all data on-device. Follow the ios-app-factory-rules. Runnable in the iOS Simulator via Xcode; provide clear run instructions.

HARD RULE ON GAPS: Anything that would need infrastructure this project cannot provide (cloud sync, shared/community decks, a deck marketplace) must NOT be faked or stubbed. Record each honestly as a gap with a short note on what building it for real would take. Do not add placeholder UI that pretends these work.

CORE FEATURES (favor complete over broad):
1. Decks & cards: create/edit/archive decks; cards have a front, back, and optional note. Card editing must be fast and keyboard-friendly.
2. Spaced-repetition scheduling: implement the SM-2 algorithm (ease factor, interval, repetition count) with Again/Hard/Good/Easy grading. THIS IS THE HEART OF THE APP. Implement it as its own standalone, pure, tested module — provably right, not plausibly right. Unit tests MUST cover: first reviews, lapses resetting the interval, ease-factor floors, and day-boundary handling in the device's local time zone (a "day" is a calendar day).
3. Review session: shows due cards for a chosen deck (or all decks); front → tap to reveal → grade. Session summary at end (cards reviewed, again-rate, time spent). Must handle interruption gracefully — quitting mid-session loses nothing.
4. Stats: per-deck and overall — due-forecast bar chart for next 30 days, daily review-count history, and retention rate (% graded Good/Easy). Handle empty and sparse data gracefully.
5. Deck import/export: export any deck to CSV; import cards from a two-column CSV (front, back) with a preview step and per-row error reporting — never silently drop a row.
6. Review reminders: one optional LOCAL notification per day ("You have N cards due") at a user-chosen time; respect permission denial gracefully. No push, no server.

PRIORITIES (in order): (1) SM-2 module correctness above all — proven via its tests; (2) review-flow speed; (3) honest empty states. Include a "demo data" toggle in Settings that seeds two decks with a realistic review history so stats screens are never empty on first look.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Let me lock down the concrete, buildable tokens and component list, and flag the technical traps in Field Ledger's signature interactions before anyone else's prose papers over them.

Starting with tokens, since that's what a SwiftUI builder actually needs to write `Theme.swift` with zero invented values. Base spacing unit is 8pt, with named steps: `xs=4` (hairline gaps, chip padding), `sm=8`, `md=16` (default screen margin and inter-row gap), `lg=24` (section breaks), `xl=32` (empty-state icon-to-title gap), `xxl=48` (top-of-screen breathing room on Decks/Stats). Corner radii: `hairline=0` (rule dividers have no radius, they're 1pt lines), `small=8` (status chips, CSV row badges), `medium=14` (deck cards, sheets, buttons), `large=24` (the full-bleed review card), `pill=999` (the four grade buttons). Type scale, all mapped to Dynamic Type styles so they actually scale: DisplayLedger 34/bold mapped to `.largeTitle` with `.monospacedDigit()` — this is the one used for the due-count stamp and retention KPI; Title 28/semibold → `.title`; Headline 20/semibold → `.title3` for deck names and section headers; Body 17/regular → `.body` for card front/back text; Secondary 13/regular → `.footnote` for metadata and timestamps; LedgerNumeral 15/medium monospaced-digit → a dedicated style used everywhere an interval, ease value, or day-count appears (deck sparkline labels, the "→ 6d" post tag, CSV row counts) so every scheduling number in the app reads with fixed-width digits, which is the actual visual mechanism that sells the ledger metaphor, not the cream background.

Colors, light/dark: background `#F7F3EA` / `#16161A`; surface (cards, sheets) `#FFFFFF` / `#1F2024`; surfaceRaised (deck card, stat card) `#FCFAF4` / `#26272C`; textPrimary `#1B1D22` / `#ECEAE2`; textSecondary `#5B5B57` / `#9C9C98`; ruleLine (row dividers) `#DAD4C4` / `#35363B`; accent/ink-blue (the one "actionable now" color — due badge, reveal button, selected grade) `#1E4D8C` / `#5B9BE0`; success (Good/Easy, retention-up) `#1E7A4C` / `#4FBE84`; warning (Hard) `#B4791E` / `#E0A34D`; error/again `#B23B3B` / `#E37272`; demoStamp `#8A1F1F` at 70% opacity / `#E06666` at 70% opacity. Every one of these needs to be an Asset Catalog color set with both appearances defined there, not a `Color(hex:)` literal scattered through views — that's what actually enforces the "one theme file" rule since Xcode will fail loudly if a named color is missing an appearance rather than silently falling back.

Now the part I actually want to push hard on, because it's an engineering trap hiding inside a design decision everyone already agreed on. The signature interaction — the 3D Y-axis card flip — has a real SwiftUI gotcha: `rotation3DEffect` rotates the same view, it doesn't swap content, so if you naively rotate one view from 0° to 180° the back face renders mirrored (readable only in a mirror) unless you swap in the back-face content exactly at the 90° midpoint and apply a compensating 180° rotation to it so it reads correctly once past the midpoint. This has to be built as two overlaid views (front/back) each with their own rotation and a `.opacity`/visibility toggle keyed to rotation angle, not one view with animated text swap. The second trap is hit-testing: whichever face is rotated past 90° and visually hidden still receives touches unless you explicitly `.disabled()` or `.allowsHitTesting(false)` it, so a fast double-tap during the flip can register on the wrong face. Both of these need to be named explicitly in the handoff or a builder will ship a flip that mirrors the back text or double-fires on quick taps.

Second engineering trap, arguably more important: the locked "session snapshot, never re-queried mid-session" rule ([REDACTED:high_entropy]) is incompatible with using SwiftData's `@Query` property wrapper inside the Review view. `@Query` is inherently live — it auto-refreshes the moment any matching model object's `nextReviewDate`/`updatedAt` changes, which is exactly what happens the instant you grade a card. If Review's queue is built with `@Query`, the "snapshot" is fiction; grading card 3 will cause SwiftData to silently re-evaluate the fetch and can reorder or drop cards from the array the view is iterating. The queue must be captured once at scope-selection time as a plain `[PersistentIdentifier]` or `[Card]` array assigned to local `@State`, built from one `FetchDescriptor` call through the shared due function, and the Review view must never re-run that fetch until scope-selection happens again. This is the single highest-risk implementation detail in the whole app relative to what's already been decided, because it's the kind of thing that compiles, looks correct in a quick demo, and then breaks under exactly the force-quit/relaunch or clock-jump test that's supposed to prove it.

Third: due-count computation for deck rows on the Decks screen must not be N separate fetches (one due-count query per deck row) — that's an N+1 pattern that'll show up as jank once someone has more than a handful of decks. The shared `dueCards(scope:)` function should back a single grouped fetch (one `FetchDescriptor` with a predicate on `nextReviewDate <= endOfLocalDay`, then bucketed by deck in memory) that Decks calls once per screen appearance, not once per row. Same discipline applies to the Stats aggregate queries — demo-exclusion needs to be a predicate condition in the fetch itself (`isDemo == false`) for aggregate views, not a post-fetch `.filter` that still pulls demo rows into memory and risks a future screen forgetting to filter them back out.

Fourth, smaller but worth locking now: the daily reminder must be scheduled as a repeating `UNCalendarNotificationTrigger` built from `DateComponents(hour:minute:)` with `repeats: true`, not a one-shot notification re-scheduled by app logic — a one-shot silently stops firing the day the user doesn't open the app, which would quietly violate "reminds you daily" the first time it matters.

Per-screen states, briefly since design_discussion already specified the copy/action pairs — my addition is what triggers each state and what "error" concretely means here, since this app has no network: Decks — empty (zero decks), populated, edit (sheet layered on populated, not a separate state), and the only real "error" state is a SwiftData save/archive failure, which should surface as an inline banner, not a full-screen error, since the underlying store failing is rare enough it shouldn't get its own dedicated screen design. Motion and haptics: card flip 400→ wait, cap is 300ms per the locked decision, `easeInOut`, interruptible (a second tap before completion should not queue a second animation, it should let the current one finish or snap). Reduce Motion swaps the 3D rotation for a same-duration crossfade — implemented via `@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion)` branching the transition, not a slower fallback. Codex, good comprehensive pass, but the coordinator's right that we can't hand a builder two different hex tables and call it done — so let me actually resolve these instead of restating my own numbers again.

On the font stack, I want to push back specifically rather than just re-asserting system fonts. Avenir Next is fine from a licensing angle since it ships preinstalled with iOS — no bundling risk there, that part of my earlier objection doesn't hold. Avenir Next doesn't expose a reliable tabular-figure variant through SwiftUI's `Font.custom` API — you'd need manual OpenType feature-tag plumbing that SwiftUI doesn't cleanly expose, and even then Avenir Next's digit widths weren't designed to guarantee tabular alignment the way SF's were. Given that both of us independently landed on "tabular numerals are the actual mechanism that sells the ledger metaphor" — not the cream background, not the accent color — picking a font that can't reliably deliver that mechanism undercuts the one thing we agreed matters most. There's also a Dynamic Type wrinkle: custom fonts need explicit `UIFontMetrics(forTextStyle:).scaledFont(for:)` wrapping to scale correctly with accessibility text sizes, versus `.system(.body, design: .default)` getting that for free. I don't see what Avenir Next buys us that's worth that cost. I'm holding my position here: system font throughout, Dynamic Type text styles, `.monospacedDigit()` on every numeral role. If you've got a specific visual reason Avenir Next matters beyond "gives it character," I want to hear it, but right now the technical case is lopsided.

## Final Output

**Design language:** Field Ledger (unchanged from design_discussion) — structure and typography only, never decoration.

### DESIGN SPEC - Type Scale
System Dynamic Type throughout — **no custom font**. Every numeral role uses `.monospacedDigit()`, which only San Francisco reliably supports; this is the actual mechanism that sells the ledger metaphor, so a font that can't guarantee it is disqualified regardless of character.
- Display/landing title: 34, semibold, `.largeTitle`, `minimumScaleFactor(0.9)` floor
- Screen title: 28, semibold, `.title`
- Section title: 22, semibold, `.title2`
- Deck name / card heading: 20, semibold, `.title3`
- Body: 17, regular, `.body`
- Body strong / action labels: 17, semibold, `.body`
- Metric values (due, interval, ease, retention, counts): 16, semibold, `.headline`, always `.monospacedDigit()`
- Secondary meta: 15, regular, `.subheadline`
- Helper text: 13, medium, `.caption`
- Small chip labels: 12, medium, `.caption`
- Empty-state title: 22, semibold, `.title2`; empty-state body: 15, regular, `.body`
- Accessibility floor: legible at AccessibilityXXL; numerals never compressed to fit — cards scroll internally instead (see Accessibility section)

### DESIGN SPEC - Spacing Grid
Base unit 4pt, Codex's finer table adopted as canonical: `s1=4, s2=8, s3=12, s4=16, s5=20, s6=24, s8=32, s10=40`. Constraint: everyday component spacing should draw from `s2/s4/s6/s8` (8/16/24/32); `s1` and `s3` are reserved narrowly for chip-internal padding and hairline row gaps, not general-purpose layout, to avoid one-off spacing drift.

### DESIGN SPEC - Corner Radii
`rSmall=8` (tags), `rMedium=12` (chips/buttons), `rLarge=18` (deck cards), `rXLarge=24` (full-screen sheets/modals), `rCircle=9999` (grade pill buttons).

### DESIGN SPEC - Semantic Color Palette
Codex's palette adopted as the base (it has more genuinely useful roles — `textTertiary`, `archivedTint`, `accentInkHigh` as a pressed/emphasis variant), with two corrections locked in:
- `surfaceBackground`: light `#F4EFE7` / dark `#0F141A`
- `surfaceCard`: light `#FFFFFF` / dark `#1A2530`
- `surfaceCanvas`: light `#FCF8F1` / dark `#14202A`
- `textPrimary`: light `#1E1B17` / dark `#F3F5F8`
- `textSecondary`: light `#5A5750` / dark `#B7BFCA`
- `textTertiary`: light `#8A857D` / dark `#8A95A5`
- `divider`: light `#E3DDD5` / dark `#2C3A48` *(fixed — Codex's original had a stray space, not a valid hex)*
- `accentInk`: light `#0E65A8` / dark `#5FB0FF`
- `accentInkHigh`: light `#084A7A` / dark `#9DD0FF`
- `success`: light `#0E8A5A` / dark `#59D9A1`
- `warning`: light `#B97F09` / dark `#F0BB46`
- `error`: light `#B02020` / dark `#F66A6A`
- `demoBadge`: light `#6B3FA0` / dark `#B98AE0` *(changed from amber to violet/plum — the original amber was one hue-step from `warning` and nearly indistinguishable from it in dark mode, which would undermine the standing unmistakable-demo-stamp requirement)*
- `archivedTint`: light `#7C8996` / dark `#98A8B6`

All five signal hues (accent-blue, success-green, warning-amber, error-red, demo-violet) are now visually distinct from each other in both appearances.

### DESIGN SPEC - Component Inventory
`FieldLedgerAppShell`, `DeckLedgerCard`, `DueCountStamp` (identical instance reused on deck rows and the Decks-screen "Review Due (N)" button — this is how the single-due-count-surface rule is enforced in code, not just in copy), `DemoDiagonalStamp`, `ReviewDueButton`, `DeckSectionHeader`, `IntervalSparkline`, `PrimaryActionButton`/`SecondaryButton`/`TextButton`, `ReviewCardSurface` + `ReviewCardFace` (front/back as two overlaid views with rotation-angle-keyed visibility swap at the 90° midpoint, plus `.allowsHitTesting(false)` on whichever face is past 90° — required to avoid mirrored back-text and double-tap misfires), `ReviewGradeRow`, `PostingTag`, `SessionProgressBadge`, `SessionSummarySheet`, `StatsMetricCard`/`RetentionKPICard`, `StatChartCard` (one shared charting shell for both the 30-day forecast and daily-history charts), `CSVImportPreviewRow`, `CSVResultSummary`, `EmptyStateBlock` (one parameterized component for every empty variant, never bespoke per screen), `ErrorStateBanner` (inline, non-blocking — there is no full-screen error state anywhere in this app), `ReminderPermissionBanner`, `ConfirmationSheet` (shared by delete-deck and disable-demo-data), `CardEditor`/`DeckEditor`/`ImportSheet`/`ExportSheet` (`ExportSheet` is just `ShareLink`, no custom screen).

### DESIGN SPEC - Navigation
Three persistent tabs: Decks (default landing), Stats, Settings. Review is not a tab — entered via a "Review Due (N)" action on Decks (all-decks scope) or a per-deck Review action, opened as `fullScreenCover`, tab bar hidden for the duration, returns to the originating tab on finish/cancel. Deck/card editors, CSV import/export, reminder explainer, and confirmations are sheets off their owning screen. Exactly one live due-count surface exists in the whole app (the Decks screen, via the shared `dueCards(scope:)` function feeding `DueCountStamp`) — no tab badge, no second counter anywhere.

### DESIGN SPEC - Per-Screen States
**Decks:** loading = 2–3 skeleton cards, no spinner/network language; empty (zero decks) = icon `books.vertical.fill`, "No decks yet," "Create your first deck to start reviewing," CTA "Create your first deck"; success = active list + collapsed archived section, each card with due stamp + sparkline + archive/demo marks; error = inline banner ("Try again" / "Troubleshoot local data"), partial data stays visible.

**Review:** entry is direct — tap "Review Due" → first card, immediately, **no loading/"Preparing due cards…" line, no interstitial** (this line is cut as a violation of the already-locked no-interstitial decision — if a fetch is ever slow enough to need one, fix the fetch, not the UI); front-hidden → revealed → mid-grade (one-frame input lock, no double-tap) → summary sheet. Two distinct empty-entry states: single-deck ("No cards due in this deck," icon `clock`, "Review another deck"/"Add cards") vs all-decks ("Nothing due across all decks," icon `calendar.badge.exclamationmark`, "Review another deck"/"Close"). Error (fetch failure mid-session): safe-exit "Return to Decks," already-graded work stays persisted.

**Stats:** loading = chart placeholders with visible axes, no spinner; empty-overall = icon `chart.bar.xaxis`, "No review history yet," "Go review due cards"; empty-per-deck = icon `rectangle.3.offgrid`, "No data for this deck"; sparse = shown honestly with a note, no fabricated smoothing; success = 30-day forecast + daily history + retention KPI, demo events excluded from aggregates via fetch predicate; error = inline banner + recompute action.

**Settings:** reminder card (not-requested/granted/denied-with-OS-Settings-deep-link), demo toggle (off/on + destructive confirmation explaining irreversible deletion on disable), CSV import (preview-before-commit, per-row status, post-commit reconciliation) and export (share sheet), and an honest gaps section (cloud sync/shared decks/marketplace). No empty state — always has content.

### DESIGN SPEC - Motion & Haptics
Card reveal: 3D Y-axis flip, 0.25–0.30s, `easeInOut`, interruptible, capped at 300ms total per the design_discussion lock. Interval-posting tag peel/fade: 0.18–0.24s, concurrent with the card filing away. Reduce Motion: same-duration crossfade, not a slower path, branched via `@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion)`. Haptics: light selection on reveal tap; distinct-but-not-alarming feedback for Again (a lapse should be felt differently, not punished); light confirmation for Hard/Good/Easy; no haptic on empty/error states.

### DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility
44×44pt minimum targets everywhere; VoiceOver labels combine control + consequence ("Good, next review in 6 days" — computed from a live SM-2 preview call, not a static string); Dynamic Type never clips or shrinks scheduling numerals — card text scrolls internally past ~3 lines at accessibility sizes via `@ScaledMetric`-driven layout, not `minimumScaleFactor`; color is never the sole signal (due/archived/demo/warning all pair with icon + text); charts always carry a textual fallback summary.

### Binding engineering constraints (locked, not optional notes)
1. The Review queue is captured once at scope-selection time as a plain array/local state from one `FetchDescriptor` call through the shared due function — **`@Query` must never be used inside the Review view**, since its live-refresh behavior would silently break the session-snapshot rule the moment a card is graded.
2. Per-deck due counts on the Decks screen come from one grouped fetch (single `FetchDescriptor`, bucketed by deck in memory), never one query per row.
3. Demo-data exclusion from aggregate Stats views is a predicate condition in the fetch itself (`isDemo == false`), never a post-fetch `.filter`.

### External design pass
**No external Claude Design pass.** The spec above is numerically complete — every token, state, and interaction constraint is explicit enough for a SwiftUI builder to write `Theme.swift` and every screen directly from this document with nothing left to invent. If stakeholder-facing mockups are ever wanted purely for pitch/buy-in purposes (not build guidance), that's a separate later ask and doesn't gate this build.

Let me lay out where I think the real landmines are, since this phase's whole job is to make tech_specs bulletproof rather than discover these mid-build.

Architecture: I want a hard module boundary, not just a code-review convention. RecallCore should be a local Swift Package (not a folder group) containing the pure SM-2 engine, the shared due-computation function, and the CSV RFC4180 parser/writer — all operating on plain structs, with zero import of SwiftData, SwiftUI, or Foundation's Date() called directly. Instead, every function that needs "now" takes an injected `Clock` (a one-method protocol returning the current Date/Calendar/TimeZone), with a `SystemClock` default and a `TestClock` the test target can freeze or advance arbitrarily. This isn't decoration — it's what makes the DST/day-boundary tests actually deterministic on CI regardless of the machine's local time zone, and it lets unit tests hit spring-forward/fall-back edge cases (the 2am hour that doesn't exist, the 1am hour that repeats twice) without touching a simulator clock at all. The one place simulator-clock-jump stays the method is the app-level integration proof already locked in detailed_discussion — that's a different, coarser test and both should exist, not one instead of the other. Making RecallCore a real SPM target means the compiler enforces the "no SwiftData/SwiftUI in the core" rule — someone can't accidentally `import SwiftData` in there even by habit, because the package doesn't link it.

At the app layer: MV over MVVM-with-ceremony — views hold `@Environment(\.modelContext)` for straightforward CRUD, but Review-queue construction and Stats aggregation go through dedicated `@Observable` services (`DueQueryService`, `SessionEngine`) so the "one shared function, never reimplemented per screen" rule is enforced by having exactly one type, not by convention. I want to flag a specific SwiftData trap here since it'll bite whoever writes the fetch predicates: SwiftData's `#Predicate` macro has real limitations with custom types — enums with associated values, computed properties, and some Optional chains don't work inside predicates as of iOS 17/18. Grade and demo-flag fields should be stored as plain `Int`/`Bool` raw values on the model, not Swift enums, or the "one grouped FetchDescriptor, no N+1" requirement from design_handoff becomes unbuildable and someone quietly falls back to post-fetch filtering, which was explicitly banned.

Second SwiftData trap, more serious because it collides with an already-locked product decision: the schema is required to stay "CloudKit-shaped" for a future sync path (per_app_product_brief), but `@Attribute(.unique)` constraints are incompatible with CloudKit-backed SwiftData stores. If anyone reaches for `.unique` on, say, a deck name to prevent duplicates, they've silently broken the future-CloudKit-readiness requirement nobody will notice until that migration is attempted. Same for non-optional relationships without defaults and any compound-key uniqueness — all forbidden by the same constraint. This needs to be an explicit rule in tech_specs, not left implicit.

Third, and this is the one I'd bet money breaks first if unstated: SwiftData's autosave is not synchronous with your mutation — it batches on the run loop. "Grade persists immediately" (DEC-prompt_contract-002) is only actually true if the grade-handling code calls `try context.save()` explicitly right after mutating the card, not if it just relies on autosave eventually flushing. Relying on autosave is exactly the kind of thing that passes a casual demo and fails the one force-quit test this whole project has staked its credibility on. I'd also push that this force-quit test be a real automated XCUITest, not a manual checklist step — `XCUIApplication().terminate()` then relaunch is a completely scriptable sequence, and given how central this guarantee is, "we checked it once by hand" isn't the bar a "provably right" project should accept.

On permissions: the only permission surface in the entire app is local notifications via `UNUserNotificationCenter`. No Info.plist usage-description string is required for that (unlike camera/location/contacts), but the toggle correctness requirement (DEC-prompt_contract-004) means the Settings screen must re-check `UNUserNotificationCenter.current().notificationSettings()` on every scenePhase transition to `.active`, not just cache what was granted at request time — a user can revoke notification permission from the OS Settings app while Recall is backgrounded, and if the toggle doesn't re-poll, it lies. Background Modes capability should stay entirely unchecked in the target — there's no background fetch, no silent push, no BGTaskScheduler work of any kind, since the reminder is a single `UNCalendarNotificationTrigger(dateMatching: DateComponents(hour:minute:), repeats: true)`, and Apple's calendar-trigger recalculates against the device's current time zone at fire time, so DST/travel are handled for free by the OS — don't reinvent that with app-side rescheduling logic.

## StoreKit 2 — In-App Purchase & Subscriptions

**Use it when:** you sell anything — consumables, non-consumables, or auto-renewable subscriptions. Replaces callback-based StoreKit 1 entirely.

**Start from:** `Product` (fetch + purchase) and `Transaction` (entitlements + history). No server strictly required — signatures are verified on-device via `VerificationResult`.

### The three things you must do

1. **Load products by ID** (IDs come from App Store Connect):

```swift
import StoreKit

let productIDs = ["com.app.pro.monthly", "com.app.pro.yearly", "com.app.coins.100"]
let products = try await Product.products(for: productIDs)   // async throws
```

2. **Purchase, then verify and finish the transaction:**

```swift
func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {
    let result = try await product.purchase()
    switch result {
    case .success(let verification):
        let transaction = try checkVerified(verification)
        await transaction.finish()          // REQUIRED — unfinished txns replay forever
        return transaction
    case .userCancelled, .pending:
        return nil
    @unknown default:
        return nil
    }
}

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant
    case .verified(let safe):       return safe
    }
}
```

3. **Listen for `Transaction.updates` from app launch** — the single most-missed requirement. It catches renewals, Ask-to-Buy approvals, refunds, and purchases made on other devices.

```swift

func observeTransactions() -> Task<Void, Never> {
    Task.detached {
        for await update in Transaction.updates {
            guard case .verified(let transaction) = update else { continue }
            await grantEntitlement(for: transaction)   // your unlock logic
            await transaction.finish()
        }
    }
}
```
